Treatment resistant jerky stiff person syndrome
T. P. Harrower, R. Barker, J. Baron, A. Coles (Cambridge, United Kingdom)
Background: Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS) is a well recognized autoimmune mediated condition with an association with antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD).

Methods: Here we present a case of a 28 male who initially presented
with neck and back pain, and generalised stiffness associated with jerks in
his neck.

Methods: Here we present a case of a 28 male who initially presented
with neck and back pain, and generalised stiffness associated with jerks in
his neck.

Immunomodulatory therapy including, steroids, plasma exchange, intravenous immunoglobulin and rituximab (monoclonal antibody directed against B cells) has
reduced the anti-GAD antibody titre to within normal limits (3. 6 ng/ml) but
has failed to produce any clinical benefit beyond a mild response to high
doses of benzodiazepines during 36 months of follow-up.

Background: Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS) is a well recognized autoimmune mediated condition with an association with antibodies to glutamic
acid decarboxylase (GAD). Less well defined is the condition of Jerky SPS,
an atypical form of SPS.

Methods: Here we present a case of a 28 male who initially presented
with neck and back pain, and generalised stiffness associated with jerks in
his neck. Over the next few months the jerky muscle activity spread to
involve his shoulder girdle (see video). Clinical examination confirmed the
presence of regular spasms resembling myoclonic jerks in the shoulder
girdle region with generalised stiffness but no other general or neurological
deficits.

Background: Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS) is a well recognized autoimmune mediated condition with an association with antibodies to glutamic
acid decarboxylase (GAD). Less well defined is the condition of Jerky SPS,
an atypical form of SPS.
Methods: Here we present a case of a 28 male who initially presented
with neck and back pain, and generalised stiffness associated with jerks in
his neck. Over the next few months the jerky muscle activity spread to
involve his shoulder girdle (see video). Clinical examination confirmed the
presence of regular spasms resembling myoclonic jerks in the shoulder
girdle region with generalised stiffness but no other general or neurological
deficits.
Results: Besides the presence of an elevated anti-GAD titre initially 12
rising to 105 (normal range less than 10 ng/ml) tests have been normal
including neuroimaging, somatosensory evoked responses. But electromyography demonstrated episodes of spontaneous motor activity. General
investigations (including tumour markers, whole body CT and FDG-PET
scanning) have failed to demonstrate an occult malignancy. Immunomodulatory therapy including, steroids, plasma exchange, intravenous immunoglobulin and rituximab (monoclonal antibody directed against B cells) has
reduced the anti-GAD antibody titre to within normal limits (3. 6 ng/ml) but
has failed to produce any clinical benefit beyond a mild response to high
doses of benzodiazepines during 36 months of follow-up.
